/Through Saturday/...
Issued at 1134 PM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

While a fairly active synoptic pattern continues across the CONUS, 
with multiple tropical systems pulling moisture northward into the 
mid-latitudes, our forecast area continues to sit just out of reach 
of the greatest tropical surges for any significant precipitation 
chances. Not all hope is lost though, as guidance continues to show 
a pattern change headed our way by midweek, with a few inches of 
snowfall on track to grace our highest elevations, and some much-needed
measurable rainfall expected for our lower elevations. 

On Sunday, an upper-level low will continue it's trek southeast out 
of the Pacific Northwest, pulling the remnants of Tropical Storm 
Rachel northeast into the Great Basin and portions of the 
Intermountain West. Both operational and ensemble guidance remain 
consistent in showing the greatest moisture largely staying west and 
north of our forecast area, with only light precipitation expected 
across our higher elevations. Southwesterly flow aloft will increase 
throughout the day, with a 65 to 75 kt 500 mb jet expected to 
straddle the UT/CO border by the early evening hours. Despite 
ensembles showing PWAT values averaging around 190% of normal, 
without the assist from any lower-level cold front or real upslope 
component, the lee side of the Front Range and plains will miss out 
on any measurable precipitation. A few hundredths can be expected
for the higher elevations, with up to .2" possible for the 
highest elevations in Jackson County. At least increased cloud 
coverage will allow for a few degrees of cooling for afternoon 
highs across the urban corridor, where low 80s are forecast, 
marking the end to any mid 80s potential for the remainder of the 
period. A few showers may linger into the late night hours, mostly
for our northern mountains where temperatures are expected to 
remain too warm for snowfall outside of potential for a dusting at
our highest mountain tops. 

For Monday, guidance remains fairly consistent across the board, 
continuing to show southwesterly flow aloft increasing as a deep 
trough remains over the western CONUS, and a closed low moving into 
northern Nevada by the evening hours. PWAT values are expected to 
drop off significantly across the lower elevations, where ensembles 
show them at 80-100% of normal, and staying around 130-150% of 
normal for the mountains and Cheyenne Ridge as the majority of 
Rachel's remnants move into the Northern Rockies. Mostly dry 
conditions are expected across the forecast area, with the 
exception of isolated afternoon showers possible for the 
mountains. Afternoon high temperatures should see a few more 
degrees knocked off before a more significant cooldown is expected
on Tuesday. Meanwhile, remnants of Hurricane Simon are expected 
to start moving northward through Mexico, getting funneled into 
the central CONUS around a high centered over the Gulf and 
aforementioned trough over the west through the week. A cold front
is expected to push south into Colorado overnight Monday that 
will cool temperatures on Tuesday to near-normal values for the 
northern plains, with warmer temperatures (5-10 degrees above 
normal) expected for Elbert and Lincoln Counties. 

Guidance continues to diverge on the evolution of the trough, 
although the 18Z ensembles stay fairly consistent through about 
Wednesday afternoon now. While there are still some details to 
iron out, we are expecting precipitation to increase Tuesday 
night, with Wednesday looking like a damp and cool day across the 
forecast area, with measurable rainfall even forecast for the 
lower elevations for the first time in a while. It's hard to 
remember the last time both the ECMWF and GFS ensembles had almost
every single member bringing QPF to the plains, and the 18Z 
output does just this. Between around 6Z Wednesday and 6Z Friday, 
we could see a few locations over the plains with around a half of
an inch of QPF, some with a little more, and some with a little 
less. At this time it does look like some upslope from the surface
to around 700 mb will help enhance precipitation totals for the 
foothills of Larimer County and the Cheyenne Ridge, but we will 
have to see if we can get some better agreement in guidance in the
next few days to dial the forecast in some more. As for our 
higher elevations, snowfall is expected, mainly above 10,000 feet,
that will likely bring our best totals of the season thus far, 
with at least a few inches expected for our northern mountains. As
for temperatures, cooler temperatures are expected to stick 
around through the week, with another cold front expected sometime
Thursday night into Friday, before a slight warmup looks on track
for next weekend.
